title: Judah’s Pledge and Joseph’s Table
summary: Pressed by famine, Jacob releases Benjamin on Judah’s pledge; the brothers find peace instead of punishment in Joseph’s house, and Joseph weeps unseen before feasting them.
historicalContext: The grain from the first journey has run out, and the famine that Joseph foretold still has years to run (45:6). A round trip from Hebron to the eastern Delta covered some two hundred and fifty miles by donkey, so each journey cost weeks and exposed the travellers to real danger. Egyptian officials of rank kept large households with stewards, store-chambers, and private rooms, and they received foreign petitioners with formal prostrations and gifts, as tomb paintings of Asiatic traders show. Jacob’s present consists of small luxury goods of the Canaanite hill country, the same kinds of resin and spice carried by the caravan that took Joseph down (37:25). The noon meal reflects Egyptian custom, where meat was a mark of wealth and honoured guests received choice portions. Egyptian reluctance to share a table with Asiatic herdsmen is reflected in ancient writers and anticipates the contempt for shepherds named in 46:34.
literaryContext: Chapters 43 to 45 form the second journey of the brothers and closely shadow the first (42:1-38): a father’s command, a descent, an audience with the lord of Egypt, and money in sacks. The parallels are deliberate, so that every difference becomes a sign of change. In the first journey Reuben’s rash offer failed; now Judah stakes himself and succeeds. Then the brothers were roughly accused; now they are fed at the governor’s house. The chapter moves from scarcity in Canaan (vv. 1-14) to abundance in Egypt (vv. 15-34), and food holds the two halves together. The key word shalom, “peace” or “welfare,” sounds at the turning point (v. 23) and in Joseph’s questions (vv. 27-28), recalling that the brothers once could not speak peaceably to him (37:4). The brothers appear simply as “the men,” for their standing as Joseph’s brothers is still under test. The feast ends in apparent calm, but chapter 44 will apply the hardest test of all.
themes: Famine and providence driving the family toward reconciliation
Faith that surrenders the outcome to God Almighty
Honesty and restitution in the face of fear
Peace announced by grace before it is understood
Hidden compassion beneath a stern exterior

outline.title: Judah Pledges Himself for Benjamin
outline.summary: With the grain gone, Judah insists that the ruler’s condition must be met and offers himself as surety for Benjamin’s safe return.

outline.title: Jacob Releases His Son to God Almighty
outline.summary: Jacob sends a present, double money, and Benjamin, commits his sons to El Shaddai’s mercy, and accepts whatever loss may come.

outline.title: Fear Answered with Peace
outline.summary: Brought into Joseph’s house, the frightened brothers explain the returned money, and the steward answers with peace, credits their God, and releases Simeon.

outline.title: Joseph Sees Benjamin
outline.summary: The eleven bow before Joseph, who asks after their father, blesses Benjamin, and withdraws to weep before composing himself.

outline.title: The Feast in Joseph’s House
outline.summary: Seated by age at separate tables, the astonished brothers watch Benjamin receive five portions and share the meal with Joseph without envy.

verses.bibleText: And the famine was sore in the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the famine was sore in the land.” Five Hebrew words carry the whole narrative forward. Jacob had closed the previous chapter with a flat refusal: Benjamin would not go down (42:38). No argument from his sons could move him. The famine does what their words could not, and the reader is meant to sense that hunger is serving a larger purpose.

The phrase echoes the famine that drove Abram into Egypt (12:10) and the one that sent Isaac toward Gerar (26:1). In each case scarcity in the land of promise forced the patriarch into a decision, and in each case God kept his hand on the family. Here the famine is the very one God had announced through Pharaoh’s dreams, so it is no blind force. Psalm 105:16 says the Lord “called for a famine upon the land,” and the next verse adds that he had already sent a man before them. The pressure on Jacob’s household and the preparation in Egypt belong to one design.

wordNotes.term: וְהָרָעָב כָּבֵד (vehara‘av kaved) — and the famine was sore
wordNotes.explanation: Kaved means “heavy” or “weighty.” Used of a famine it describes something that presses down on a land and its people. The same adjective marks the famine of Abram’s day as “grievous” (12:10) and Joseph’s warning that the coming dearth would be “very grievous” (41:31). Elsewhere it describes a hand of judgment laid heavily on a people (1 Samuel 5:6). The word suggests a burden that will not lift of its own accord.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when they had eaten up the corn which they had brought out of Egypt, their father said unto them, Go again, buy us a little food.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Months have passed. The grain brought from Egypt, which had to feed a large clan with servants and flocks, is gone. The narrator does not say how long the family waited, but Judah will later remark that they could have made the journey twice over (v. 10), so the delay was long and deliberate. Jacob held out as long as he could.

When he finally speaks, his words are noticeably smaller than before. In the first journey he chided his sons for staring at one another and laid out the need at length (42:1-2). Now he says only, “Go again, buy us a little food.” The word “little” is telling. Jacob seems to hope that a modest request will slip past the obstacle everyone knows is waiting, as though the man in Egypt might sell a small amount without asking for Benjamin. He does not mention Simeon, still held as a hostage, nor the condition the ruler laid down. Grief and fear have made him avoid the hard subject. He speaks as though the problem might simply go away if no one names it.

The verse shows how a person can know what God’s providence requires and still try to negotiate around it. Jacob is the head of the family and gives the command, but the real decision has already been made by the famine. The coming conversation will strip away his evasion.

wordNotes.term: שֻׁבוּ שִׁבְרוּ־לָנוּ מְעַט־אֹכֶל (shuvu shivru-lanu me‘at-’okhel) — go again, buy us a little food
wordNotes.explanation: Shuvu, “return,” recalls the first journey, and shivru is the verb used for buying grain throughout the famine narrative (42:2-3). Me‘at, “a little,” softens the request. The same phrase returns when Judah later recounts this scene to Joseph (44:25), showing that the brothers remembered how their father tried to minimize what was at stake.

verses.bibleText: And Judah spake unto him, saying, The man did solemnly protest unto us, saying, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Judah spake unto him.” For the first time Judah takes the lead in speaking to his father. Reuben, the firstborn, had already been rebuffed (42:37-38); Simeon was in prison in Egypt; Levi shared Simeon’s guilt at Shechem (34:25-30). Judah, fourth in line, is the son who can still be heard. From this point on he becomes the voice of the brothers (44:14-18; 46:28), and Jacob’s final blessing will confirm his leadership (49:8-10).

Judah does not argue with Jacob’s wish for food. He simply restates the fact that makes the trip impossible on Jacob’s terms. “The man did solemnly protest unto us.” The brothers call the governor “the man” throughout, not knowing his name, and certainly not his identity. Judah’s summary is a free retelling of 42:15-20, compressing the ruler’s words into one sharp sentence: “Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you.” To be denied the face of the man who controlled Egypt’s grain was to be denied food itself.

There is irony beneath the surface. The face the brothers cannot see without Benjamin is the face of the brother they sold. Joseph’s demand presses them toward the very son of Rachel who might expose any lingering jealousy. Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph for profit (37:26-27), now plainly faces his father with an unwelcome truth.

wordNotes.term: הָעֵד הֵעִד (ha‘ed he‘id) — did solemnly protest
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is doubled for emphasis: literally “warning, he warned.” The form means to testify against someone or to give a solemn charge with consequences attached. Moses uses the same doubled construction when he warns Israel that forgetting the Lord will bring ruin (Deuteronomy 8:19), and Samuel is told to warn the people solemnly about the ways of a king (1 Samuel 8:9). Judah presents the ruler’s condition as binding, not negotiable.

wordNotes.term: לֹא־תִרְאוּ פָנַי (lo-tir’u fanay) — ye shall not see my face
wordNotes.explanation: To see a ruler’s face meant to be admitted to his presence and favour. Absalom lived in Jerusalem two years without seeing the king’s face, a sign of banishment (2 Samuel 14:24), and Pharaoh threatened Moses with death if he saw his face again (Exodus 10:28). For the brothers, exclusion from the man’s presence meant no grain.

verses.bibleText: If thou wilt send our brother with us, we will go down and buy thee food:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Judah sets out the alternatives with plain logic. The first half of his statement is conditional and positive: “If thou wilt send our brother with us, we will go down and buy thee food.” He puts the decision squarely in his father’s hands. The sons, grown men with families of their own, could have taken Benjamin and gone, but they do not act without Jacob’s consent. Authority in Canaan still rests with the patriarch, even while authority over grain rests with the man in Egypt.

Judah also reframes the matter. Jacob spoke of “us” needing food; Judah speaks of buying food for “thee.” The journey is for Jacob’s sake, and the cost of refusing will fall on him too. The phrase “our brother” is also worth noticing. Benjamin is not only Jacob’s cherished son; he belongs to the brothers, and they now speak of him with a family claim that they never extended to Joseph.

wordNotes.term: אִם־יֶשְׁךָ מְשַׁלֵּחַ (’im-yeshkha meshalleach) — if thou wilt send
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “if there is you sending,” using the particle yesh, “there is,” with a participle. The construction highlights the existence of a settled will to act. Abraham’s servant uses the same idiom when asking whether God will truly prosper his errand (24:42). The negative counterpart follows in verse 5.

verses.bibleText: But if thou wilt not send him, we will not go down: for the man said unto us, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second half of Judah’s statement mirrors the first: “But if thou wilt not send him, we will not go down.” The balanced structure leaves no third way. Judah repeats the ruler’s words a second time, word for word, so that Jacob cannot treat them as exaggeration: “Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you.”

This is firm speech from a son to a father in a culture that honoured paternal authority. Judah is not defiant, but he refuses to make a journey that he knows would end in failure, imprisonment, or worse. A second trip without Benjamin would confirm the charge of spying (42:16) and might cost Simeon his life. Respect for a parent does not mean pretending that an impossible plan can work. Judah honours his father best by telling him the truth, however unwelcome, and leaving the decision with him.

wordNotes.term: וְאִם־אֵינְךָ מְשַׁלֵּחַ (ve’im-’enkha meshalleach) — but if thou wilt not send
wordNotes.explanation: The negative particle ’en, “there is not,” answers yesh in verse 4: if the willingness to send is absent, the journey is off. The paired construction forms a deliberate either-or, like the choice Laban’s household put to Abraham’s servant (24:49). Judah gives his father two doors and closes neither one by force.

verses.bibleText: And Israel said, Wherefore dealt ye so ill with me, as to tell the man whether ye had yet a brother?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Israel said.” The narrator switches from “their father” (v. 2) to his covenant name, Israel, as he speaks in his role as head of the clan. Yet what Israel says sounds more like the old Jacob. He does not answer Judah’s logic; he turns on all his sons together: “Wherefore dealt ye so ill with me, as to tell the man whether ye had yet a brother?”

The complaint is unfair. The brothers could hardly have hidden their family from a ruler who was questioning them as suspected spies. But grief rarely reasons. Jacob has already accused them of bereaving him (42:36), and now he hears in this new crisis a repetition of the old one. The verb he uses, built on the word for “evil,” recalls the “evil beast” that supposedly devoured Joseph (37:20, 33). Without saying it, Jacob suspects that his sons are once again the cause of his losses, and in a way he does not know, he is right about the past.

The question also reveals a man who sees every event as aimed at himself: “dealt ye so ill with me.” Earlier he cried, “all these things are against me” (42:36). He has not yet seen that God is working all these things together for good. Moses later uses the same verb when he asks the Lord why he has “afflicted” his servant (Numbers 11:11), and the pattern is familiar: a burdened servant of God mistakes the road to deliverance for a road to ruin.

wordNotes.term: לָמָה הֲרֵעֹתֶם לִי (lamah hare‘otem li) — wherefore dealt ye so ill with me
wordNotes.explanation: Hare‘otem is a causative form related to ra‘, “evil, harm.” It means to bring trouble on someone or treat them badly. Moses uses it in protest to God after Pharaoh increases Israel’s burdens (Exodus 5:22) and again under the weight of leading the people (Numbers 11:11). The word links Jacob’s accusation with the “evil beast” of 37:20, a story the brothers knew to be false.

verses.bibleText: And they said, The man asked us straitly of our state, and of our kindred, saying, Is your father yet alive? have ye another brother? and we told him according to the tenor of these words: could we certainly know that he would say, Bring your brother down?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers answer together, defending their honesty. “The man asked us straitly of our state, and of our kindred.” They describe a pointed interrogation, and they quote two of the man’s questions: “Is your father yet alive? have ye another brother?” These questions do not appear in the narrator’s account of the first audience (42:9-16), where the brothers seem to volunteer their family details. Judah will repeat the same version to Joseph himself (44:19), who knew exactly what had been said, so the brothers are not inventing an excuse. The narrator simply left some of the exchange unrecorded in chapter 42 and supplies it now through their mouths.

Their reply ends with a question of their own: “could we certainly know that he would say, Bring your brother down?” It is a fair point and carries a note of exasperation, perhaps even a hint of reproach toward their father. They answered “according to the tenor of these words,” replying to exactly what was asked. No one could have foreseen that an honest answer would produce such a demand.

The exchange shows the brothers in a new light. Years earlier they deceived their father with a bloodied robe and silence (37:31-35). Now they insist that they told the truth, and the narrative supports them. It is a small sign that something is changing. The reader also knows what the brothers do not: Joseph asked about the father because he longed to know whether Jacob lived, and about the brother because he wanted to see whether Rachel’s other son had suffered his own fate. Questions that felt like interrogation came from a brother’s heart.

wordNotes.term: שָׁאוֹל שָׁאַל־הָאִישׁ (sha’ol sha’al-ha’ish) — the man asked us straitly
wordNotes.explanation: The verb sha’al, “to ask,” is doubled for intensity: “the man asked and asked,” questioning closely and persistently. The same doubled form describes David pressing Jonathan for leave (1 Samuel 20:6, 28). The brothers stress that they were cross-examined, not careless.

wordNotes.term: הֲיָדוֹעַ נֵדַע (hayadoa‘ neda‘) — could we certainly know
wordNotes.explanation: Another doubled verb, this time in a rhetorical question: “knowing, could we know?” The expected answer is no. The same emphatic form appears when Joseph later asks whether they did not know that a man like him could certainly divine (44:15). Human foresight is limited; only God sees the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10).

verses.bibleText: And Judah said unto Israel his father, Send the lad with me, and we will arise and go; that we may live, and not die, both we, and thou, and also our little ones.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Judah steps back into the conversation, and the narrator names the relationship with care: “Judah said unto Israel his father.” The brothers’ defence in verse 7 risked prolonging the quarrel; Judah moves past blame to a proposal. “Send the lad with me.” The appeal is personal. Benjamin is to go not merely with the group but under Judah’s own charge.

Calling Benjamin “the lad” does not mean he was a child. He was born before Joseph was sold more than twenty years earlier (35:16-18), so he was a grown man, and the list of his sons in 46:21 shows he already had a family. The word na‘ar marks his position as the youngest and most protected son, the one Jacob still treated as a boy. Joseph will address him affectionately in a similar way, calling him “my son” (v. 29).

Judah then raises the stakes beyond Benjamin: “that we may live, and not die, both we, and thou, and also our little ones.” He echoes Jacob’s own words from the first journey, when the father sent them to buy grain “that we may live, and not die” (42:2). Now the phrase turns back on him. Refusing to send Benjamin will not keep anyone safe; it will doom three generations. Judah widens Jacob’s view from the one son he fears to lose to the whole family whose survival hangs on his decision. Naming the little ones last reminds Jacob that his grandchildren have as strong a claim on his care as Benjamin does.

The argument is forthright and sober, without the theatrical oath Reuben offered. It also marks a shift in Judah himself. The son who once separated from his brothers and went down to the Canaanites (38:1) now speaks as the one who holds the family together. God has been at work in him since the events at Timnah, when he confessed of Tamar, “She hath been more righteous than I” (38:26).

wordNotes.term: הַנַּעַר (hanna‘ar) — the lad
wordNotes.explanation: Na‘ar is a flexible word covering an infant (Exodus 2:6), a youth (37:2), or a young man of fighting age or in service (14:24; 41:12). It often expresses social position rather than age, marking a junior or dependent. Benjamin was a married adult, yet within his father’s household he remained “the lad,” the youngest and most guarded son. The word recurs repeatedly in Judah’s later plea (44:22, 30-34).

wordNotes.term: וְנִחְיֶה וְלֹא נָמוּת (venichyeh velo’ namut) — that we may live, and not die
wordNotes.explanation: The paired positive and negative form a strong expression of survival. Jacob used it when first sending his sons (42:2), and the Egyptians will use it when they come to Joseph with nothing left to sell but themselves (47:19). Moses later sets before Israel a choice between life and death (Deuteronomy 30:19), and the same contrast underlies Christ’s promise that whoever believes in him should not perish (John 3:16).

verses.bibleText: I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him: if I bring him not unto thee, and set him before thee, then let me bear the blame for ever:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him.” The Hebrew puts the pronoun first and adds emphasis: “I myself will be surety.” Judah binds his own person to Benjamin’s safety. A surety in the ancient world was one who stood in another’s place, answering for a debt or obligation with his own goods or life if the other failed. Judah offers exactly that. If Benjamin does not return, his father may hold Judah accountable.

The contrast with Reuben is sharp. Reuben had said, “Slay my two sons, if I bring him not to thee” (42:37), an offer that only promised Jacob the loss of more grandsons. Judah puts no one forward but himself. He adds, “if I bring him not unto thee, and set him before thee, then let me bear the blame for ever.” The phrase means literally “I will have sinned against you all the days.” He accepts lifelong guilt before his father, with whatever consequences that may carry, should he fail. Later, when the moment of testing comes, Judah will make good on this pledge before Joseph, offering to remain as a slave in Benjamin’s place and recalling these very words (44:32-33).

There is a striking echo from Judah’s own past. The noun for “pledge” built on the same root appeared when Judah gave Tamar his seal, cord, and staff as security (38:17-18). Then the pledge served his own appetite and nearly cost an innocent woman her life. Now he pledges himself to save his brother. Proverbs warns against becoming surety for a stranger (Proverbs 6:1-5; 11:15), but Judah is not making a careless business promise; he is giving himself for his own brother so that the family may live.

Dothan stands behind these words as well. There it was Judah who asked, “What profit is it if we slay our brother?” and proposed selling Joseph instead (37:26-27). He spared one son of Rachel only to turn him into silver. Now he puts his own life up as security for Rachel’s other son.

Scripture uses this very idea of Christ. Hebrews 7:22 calls Jesus “a surety of a better testament.” The Greek word there means a guarantor, one who stakes himself to make an agreement good. Judah could only promise; Christ fulfils. Judah offered his freedom; Christ gave his life, bearing the penalty of sin in the place of those he represents. The psalmist’s prayer, “Be surety for thy servant for good” (Psalm 119:122), finds its answer in the Son of Judah’s tribe who has bound himself to bring his brethren safely home to the Father (Hebrews 2:10-13).

wordNotes.term: אָנֹכִי אֶעֶרְבֶנּוּ (’anokhi ’e‘ervennu) — I will be surety for him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb ‘arav means to stand as guarantor, to become liable for another. It describes taking responsibility for a neighbour’s debt (Proverbs 6:1; 11:15) and appears in Hezekiah’s cry, “undertake for me” (Isaiah 38:14), and the psalmist’s plea, “Be surety for thy servant” (Psalm 119:122). The related noun ‘eravon, “pledge,” was used of the tokens Judah left with Tamar (38:17-18). The emphatic pronoun ’anokhi stresses that Judah himself, not his sons or brothers, is the security.

wordNotes.term: וְחָטָאתִי לְךָ כָּל־הַיָּמִים (vechata’ti lekha kol-hayyamim) — then let me bear the blame for ever
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “and I will have sinned against you all the days.” Chata’, “to sin, to miss the mark,” here means to be counted guilty and liable to the consequences. Bathsheba uses the same idea when she fears that she and Solomon will be “counted offenders” (1 Kings 1:21). Judah repeats this oath to Joseph (44:32), showing that he regarded it as binding.

verses.bibleText: For except we had lingered, surely now we had returned this second time.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Judah closes with a blunt remark that sounds almost like a reproach: “For except we had lingered, surely now we had returned this second time.” The delay has been costly. While Jacob hesitated, food dwindled, Simeon sat in an Egyptian prison, and nothing changed except that the danger grew.

The word for lingering is the one used of Lot as he dawdled in Sodom while the angels urged him to flee (19:16). Delay in the face of a clear duty is never neutral. The psalmist resolves, “I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments” (Psalm 119:60). Judah is not impatient for its own sake; he is confident that the journey can succeed and that further hesitation serves no one. His words carry the expectation of a safe return, a hope Jacob has not yet allowed himself.

The remark also reveals Judah’s expectation of success. He speaks of a completed round trip, not of disaster on the road or a dungeon in Egypt. Faith sometimes looks like plain good sense that refuses to be frozen by fear: Judah has weighed the danger and judged that facing the necessity God has set before the family is safer than waiting.

wordNotes.term: הִתְמַהְמָהְנוּ (hitmahmahnu) — we had lingered
wordNotes.explanation: The verb mahah, in this reflexive form, means to hesitate, delay, or drag one’s feet. It describes Lot lingering in Sodom (19:16), Israel unable to “tarry” as they left Egypt (Exodus 12:39), and the psalmist who refused to delay obedience (Psalm 119:60). Judah names his father’s indecision honestly.

verses.bibleText: And their father Israel said unto them, If it must be so now, do this; take of the best fruits in the land in your vessels, and carry down the man a present, a little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“If it must be so now, do this.” Jacob concedes. There is no recorded word of agreement with Judah’s pledge, only the acknowledgement that no other way remains. Once he yields, however, the old resourcefulness returns. The man who once sent waves of gifts ahead to soften Esau (32:13-21) now prepares a present to win favour with the ruler of Egypt.

The gift is drawn from “the best fruits in the land,” products of Canaan’s hill country that Egypt did not produce in abundance: balm, honey, spices, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds. Several of these are the very goods carried by the Ishmaelite caravan that took Joseph down to Egypt (37:25). The brothers will unknowingly hand their brother the same cargo that travelled with him into slavery. Even in famine, such items could be kept in small quantities, and their value lay in rarity, not bulk. Jacob twice says “a little,” and the modesty of the amounts matches the scarcity of the times.

The honey may have been the thick syrup made by boiling down grape juice or dates, a product still traded from the Hebron region, though wild bees’ honey from rocks and trees is also possible (Deuteronomy 32:13). Pistachio nuts appear only here in the Bible; almonds grew well in Canaan but were scarce in Egypt.

The word for the present, minchah, is the same word used for Cain’s and Abel’s offerings (4:3-5) and for Jacob’s gift to Esau (32:13; 33:10). It is the tribute brought by a lesser party to a greater one, a sign of respect and a request for goodwill. Proverbs observes that a man’s gift “maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men” (Proverbs 18:16). Jacob is doing what prudence can do while leaving the outcome to God. His careful preparation does not contradict the prayer that follows in verse 14. Diligence and dependence on God are partners, and the man who does what lies in his power is the one best placed to commit the rest to the Lord.

wordNotes.term: מִנְחָה (minchah) — a present
wordNotes.explanation: Minchah is a gift or tribute brought to a superior to show honour and seek favour. It names the offerings of Cain and Abel (4:3-4), the present Jacob sent to Esau (32:13, 20; 33:10), and tribute paid by subject kings (1 Kings 4:21). In the law it becomes the term for the grain offering (Leviticus 2:1). In this chapter it frames the brothers’ approach to Joseph (vv. 15, 25-26).

wordNotes.term: מִזִּמְרַת הָאָרֶץ (mizzimrat ha’arets) — of the best fruits in the land
wordNotes.explanation: Zimrah occurs only here in this sense and denotes the choice produce for which a land is celebrated. Context determines the meaning: Jacob lists the finest goods Canaan could offer. Compare the spies’ display of the land’s fruit (Numbers 13:23) and the description of Canaan as a land of “honey” and choice yield (Deuteronomy 8:8).

verses.bibleText: And take double money in your hand; and the money that was brought again in the mouth of your sacks, carry it again in your hand; peradventure it was an oversight:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And take double money in your hand.” Jacob’s instructions turn from gifts to payment. The brothers are to carry enough silver to buy new grain and also to return the money they found in their sacks after the first journey (42:27-28, 35). The phrase “in your hand” appears twice, stressing that the money is to be openly carried and openly offered, not hidden away.

The returned money had terrified them. When it first appeared, they asked one another, “What is this that God hath done unto us?” (42:28). Jacob now suggests a more ordinary explanation: “peradventure it was an oversight.” Perhaps an Egyptian official had simply erred. Whatever the cause, keeping silver that was not theirs would be dishonest, and it could also be used as evidence against them. The family that bore God’s promise was to deal uprightly even when the error had worked in their favour.

Jacob’s word “peradventure” also hints at uncertainty. He does not know what to make of the money, and he may still half suspect his sons. Yet his instruction is clear: make restitution in full. The principle later written into Israel’s law is already at work, that what belongs to another must be restored (Leviticus 6:4-5). Zacchaeus showed the fruit of a changed heart in the same way (Luke 19:8). The brothers will obey their father to the letter, and their honesty about the money will become the first thing they say on arriving in Egypt (vv. 20-22).

wordNotes.term: מִשְׁגֶּה (mishgeh) — an oversight
wordNotes.explanation: Mishgeh, found only here, comes from shagah, “to go astray, to err.” Related words describe unintentional sins for which the law provided sacrifices (Leviticus 4:2, 13; Numbers 15:27). Jacob hopes the money was returned by an innocent mistake, not as a trap. Ecclesiastes uses a related noun of an error that proceeds from a ruler (Ecclesiastes 10:5).

verses.bibleText: Take also your brother, and arise, go again unto the man:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Take also your brother.” After the gifts and the money, Jacob finally names the one thing that matters. The Hebrew places “your brother” first for emphasis: “and your brother, take!” He does not say “Benjamin,” and he does not say “my son,” as he had in 42:38. He speaks of “your brother,” perhaps unable to bring himself to say the name, and perhaps also reminding his sons that Benjamin is their brother, entrusted to them as Joseph once was.

Then comes the command: “arise, go again unto the man.” The same verbs Judah used in verse 8, “arise and go,” now come from Jacob’s lips. The father has accepted his son’s plan. The phrase “go again” recalls verse 2, but now the obstacle is removed. What Jacob refused in 42:38 he grants here, and the turning point of the family’s story has been reached in a single short sentence.

wordNotes.term: וְאֶת־אֲחִיכֶם קָחוּ (ve’et-’achikhem qachu) — take also your brother
wordNotes.explanation: The object stands before the verb, giving it weight: “your brother, take him.” Jacob calls him their brother, not his son, placing responsibility on them. Years earlier he sent Joseph to see the welfare of “thy brethren” (37:14); now the brothers are charged with the welfare of their youngest. Cain’s question, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (4:9), receives a different answer in this family.

verses.bibleText: And God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may send away your other brother, and Benjamin. If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob’s final words are a blessing and a surrender. “And God Almighty give you mercy before the man.” He calls on God by the name El Shaddai, the name by which God revealed himself to Abraham when he promised a multitude of descendants (17:1-2), the name Isaac used in blessing Jacob as he fled to Haran (28:3), and the name God himself spoke at Bethel when he renewed the covenant (35:11). In invoking it now, Jacob reaches back to the promises. The God who pledged to make his family a nation will not let it perish in a famine.

He asks specifically for “mercy before the man.” Jacob understands that the heart of Egypt’s ruler is in God’s hand (Proverbs 21:1). Solomon later prays that God would give captive Israel compassion before their captors (1 Kings 8:50), and Nehemiah asks for mercy “in the sight of this man” before the Persian king (Nehemiah 1:11). The irony is rich: the man before whom Jacob seeks compassion is his own son, whose compassion will overflow before the day is out (v. 30). The same Hebrew word stands behind both verses.

Jacob also prays that the man will “send away your other brother, and Benjamin.” Simeon is still unnamed, “your other brother,” while Benjamin is named. The old favouritism lingers. Yet Jacob does ask for both, and for the first time Simeon’s release appears in his words.

Then comes the cry: “If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved.” The words have been heard as despair, and they certainly carry the weight of an old man who has lost Rachel, Joseph, and now perhaps Simeon and Benjamin. But they follow a prayer, and they are the language of one who has stopped trying to control what he cannot control. Esther will speak in a similar way as she goes uninvited to the king: “if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16). Jacob’s faith is not heroic, but it is real. He places his sons in God’s hands and accepts whatever God permits.

In fact God intends not to bereave Jacob but to restore to him the son he thought dead. Jacob gives up Benjamin and receives back both Benjamin and Joseph. Paul’s assurance that the God who spared not his own Son will with him freely give us all things (Romans 8:32) stands behind every such surrender.

wordNotes.term: וְאֵל שַׁדַּי יִתֵּן לָכֶם רַחֲמִים (ve’El Shadday yitten lakhem rachamim) — and God Almighty give you mercy
wordNotes.explanation: El Shaddai is the patriarchal name of God tied to the covenant promise of fruitfulness (17:1; 28:3; 35:11; 48:3). Rachamim, “mercy” or “compassion,” is related to rechem, “womb,” and describes tender, feeling love. The plural intensifies it. The same noun returns in verse 30, where Joseph’s compassion (rachamav) is stirred toward Benjamin, so Jacob’s prayer is answered within the chapter by the very man he fears.

wordNotes.term: כַּאֲשֶׁר שָׁכֹלְתִּי שָׁכָלְתִּי (ka’asher shakholti shakhalti) — if I be bereaved, I am bereaved
wordNotes.explanation: Shakhol means to be bereft of children. Rebekah feared being “deprived” of both sons in one day (27:45), and Jacob used the word bitterly in 42:36: “Me have ye bereaved.” The repetition expresses resignation to an outcome beyond one’s control, like Esther’s “if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16). Here it follows prayer, giving it the tone of surrender to God’s will more than fatalism.

verses.bibleText: And the men took that present, and they took double money in their hand, and Benjamin; and rose up, and went down to Egypt, and stood before Joseph.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The verse records obedience in the very words of the command. “The men took that present, and they took double money in their hand, and Benjamin.” Each item Jacob named in verses 11-13 is now ticked off. The brothers do exactly as their father said, without improvising or cutting corners. Benjamin is listed last, almost as though he were one more item of cargo, yet he is the reason the whole journey can happen.

The long trek of several weeks is compressed into a handful of verbs: they “rose up, and went down to Egypt, and stood before Joseph.” The narrator hurries the journey so that he can slow the encounter. From here on the story moves almost scene by scene, with fears, conversations, and gestures given in detail.

The last phrase, “stood before Joseph,” is weighted. The brothers think they stand before an Egyptian lord; the reader knows they stand before the brother they sold. To stand before someone is the posture of servants awaiting orders, as Joseph himself once stood before Pharaoh (41:46). The roles foreseen in the dreams of chapter 37 are now fixed in place, though only one person in the room knows it. From this verse onward the brothers are called “the men,” not “Joseph’s brethren,” because whether they will truly act as brothers is the question still to be answered.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּעַמְדוּ לִפְנֵי יוֹסֵף (vayya‘amdu lifne Yosef) — and stood before Joseph
wordNotes.explanation: To “stand before” someone is the language of attendance on a superior, used of servants before a master and officials before a king. Joseph “stood before Pharaoh” when he entered royal service (41:46), and the queen of Sheba called Solomon’s servants happy who “stand continually before thee” (1 Kings 10:8). Proverbs says a skilful man “shall stand before kings” (Proverbs 22:29).

verses.bibleText: And when Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the ruler of his house, Bring these men home, and slay, and make ready; for these men shall dine with me at noon.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when Joseph saw Benjamin with them.” The first thing Joseph notices is not the gifts or the money but the presence of his younger brother. Benjamin’s arrival proves that the brothers have kept their word, that Jacob is alive enough to send him, and that Rachel’s other son has not met Joseph’s fate. Whatever Joseph felt, he controlled it in public and turned to practical orders.

He speaks to “the ruler of his house,” his chief steward, the same kind of position Joseph himself once held in Potiphar’s house (39:4). The orders are surprising: “Bring these men home, and slay, and make ready; for these men shall dine with me at noon.” The brothers expected to buy grain at the public store. Instead they are to be taken into the governor’s private residence for a meal. Slaughtering an animal for guests marked a feast of honour; meat was costly, especially in famine, and was served when hospitality was meant to impress.

Joseph’s purposes are layered. He wants to watch his brothers closely in a relaxed setting, especially how they treat Benjamin. He also wants to give them food and kindness, which he has longed to do. The noon meal will become the stage for a new test. Wisdom literature describes a host who “hath killed her beasts” and “furnished her table” to invite guests to her house (Proverbs 9:1-2); here a wise man prepares a table, and the guests do not yet know whose wisdom they are about to taste.

wordNotes.term: לַאֲשֶׁר עַל־בֵּיתוֹ (la’asher ‘al-beto) — to the ruler of his house
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to the one who is over his house,” a standard title for a chief steward. Joseph was set “over his house” by Potiphar (39:4) and by Pharaoh (41:40). In Israel the title marked a high palace official such as Shebna (Isaiah 22:15). The same steward will carry out Joseph’s orders with the silver cup (44:1).

wordNotes.term: וּטְבֹחַ טֶבַח וְהָכֵן (utevoach tevach vehakhen) — and slay, and make ready
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “slaughter a slaughtering and prepare.” Tavach is the ordinary verb for butchering meat for a meal, used of Wisdom preparing her feast (Proverbs 9:2) and Nabal’s meat prepared for his shearers (1 Samuel 25:11). It is related to the title of Potiphar, “captain of the guard” (37:36), but here it simply describes preparing a banquet.

verses.bibleText: And the man did as Joseph bade; and the man brought the men into Joseph's house.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The steward obeys promptly: “the man did as Joseph bade; and the man brought the men into Joseph’s house.” The sentence is plain, but its repetition of “the man” and “the men” slows the pace and draws attention to the move from the public grain market to the private house.

The brothers had previously met Joseph in an official setting and spent three days in custody (42:17). Being led into a ruler’s house was another matter altogether. In the open field at Dothan they had held Joseph in their power (37:23-24); now they are taken inside his walls, where he holds all the power and they have no means of escape. The reader knows the invitation is kind. The brothers know only that they have been singled out.

The steward is a minor figure, yet a faithful one. He carries out his master’s orders exactly, and in the scenes that follow he will speak and act for Joseph with a blend of kindness and firmness (v. 23; 44:1-10). Joseph had once served an Egyptian house in just this way; now he has such a servant of his own.

wordNotes.term: בֵּיתָה יוֹסֵף (betah Yosef) — into Joseph’s house
wordNotes.explanation: The directional ending marks movement toward the house. In the Joseph narrative, “house” traces his path: from Jacob’s house, to Potiphar’s house (39:2), to the prison house (39:20), and finally to his own house as ruler (41:40). The brothers now enter the household of the brother they sold.

verses.bibleText: And the men were afraid, because they were brought into Joseph's house; and they said, Because of the money that was returned in our sacks at the first time are we brought in; that he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us, and take us for bondmen, and our asses.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the men were afraid, because they were brought into Joseph’s house.” Their fear follows naturally. Other buyers took their grain and left; these Canaanites alone were led into the governor’s residence. In their minds there could be only one reason: the money returned in their sacks on the first trip. They assume the invitation is a pretext. “That he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us, and take us for bondmen, and our asses.”

The language piles up verbs of attack. Literally they fear that the man will “roll himself upon us” and “throw himself upon us,” a picture of being overwhelmed by a sudden assault. High officials in Egypt kept detention rooms in their houses (40:3), and the brothers had already spent three days in custody. Their worry about losing their donkeys seems almost comic, since the lord of Egypt hardly needed their pack animals, but fear does not think in proportions. For men whose whole livelihood walked on four legs, a handful of donkeys was all that stood between their households and ruin.

The deeper reason for their alarm is a guilty conscience. Men who once seized their brother, stripped him, and sold him as a slave (37:23-28) now fear that they will be seized and enslaved. They had already confessed, “We are verily guilty concerning our brother” (42:21). Every unexplained event since then has seemed like retribution. Scripture observes that “the wicked flee when no man pursueth” (Proverbs 28:1). The brothers are not fleeing, but they read kindness as threat because they know what they deserve.

There is grace in the misunderstanding. The fear that grips them drives them to the steward with confession and restitution before anyone accuses them. God often uses an awakened conscience to bring people to honesty, so that when mercy arrives it is received and not presumed upon.

wordNotes.term: לְהִתְגֹּלֵל עָלֵינוּ וּלְהִתְנַפֵּל עָלֵינוּ (lehitgolel ‘alenu ulhitnappel ‘alenu) — that he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us
wordNotes.explanation: The first verb, from galal, “to roll,” occurs in this reflexive form only here; it pictures someone rolling down upon another, overwhelming them. Job uses a related form of calamities that “rolled themselves upon me” (Job 30:14). The second verb, from naphal, “to fall,” means to attack. Together they express dread of a sudden assault. The brothers fear being made ‘avadim, “bondmen,” the very fate they inflicted on Joseph (37:27-28).

verses.bibleText: And they came near to the steward of Joseph's house, and they communed with him at the door of the house,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Before they are taken further in, the brothers approach the steward. “They came near to the steward of Joseph’s house, and they communed with him at the door of the house.” The setting is significant. At the threshold they can still state their case before entering the place where they fear they will be trapped.

The verb “came near” is the same one used when Judah later approaches Joseph to plead for Benjamin (44:18), and when Joseph calls his brothers to come near and see that he is their brother (45:4). Drawing near takes courage when one feels guilty. The brothers do not wait to be accused; they go to the official first and speak. That initiative is itself a sign of honesty. Men who intended to keep stolen money would have stayed silent.

Speaking up at the door, before anyone has charged them, is wiser than waiting to be found out. Scripture ties mercy to that kind of openness: “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). The brothers are learning the lesson one step at a time.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּגְּשׁוּ (vayyiggeshu) — and they came near
wordNotes.explanation: Nagash means to approach, often to present a request or face a superior. It marks the decisive moments of the coming chapters: Judah “came near” to plead (44:18), and Joseph invites his brothers, “Come near to me” (45:4). Abraham likewise “drew near” to intercede for Sodom (18:23).

verses.bibleText: And said, O sir, we came indeed down at the first time to buy food:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“O sir, we came indeed down at the first time to buy food.” The brothers open with a respectful plea and a statement of their original purpose. The doubled verb in Hebrew, “going down, we went down,” stresses their sincerity: they truly came only to buy, not to steal or spy.

The phrase “O sir” renders a polite particle of entreaty, a way of begging the listener’s indulgence before speaking. Judah will open his great appeal to Joseph with the same expression (44:18). It is the language of people who know they are at the mercy of the one they address. The brothers’ manner has changed since Dothan, where they ignored Joseph’s pleading entirely (42:21). Now they are the ones asking for a hearing.

Their statement is brief and factual. They make no excuses and do not speculate about how the money came to be in their sacks. They simply establish that their first visit was legitimate. Truthful speech that begins with plain facts is the proper start of any honest account.

wordNotes.term: בִּי אֲדֹנִי (bi ’adoni) — O sir
wordNotes.explanation: Bi is a particle of polite entreaty, roughly “please, my lord,” used to introduce a request to a superior with deference. Judah uses it to open his plea (44:18), Aaron uses it before Moses (Numbers 12:11), Hannah before Eli (1 Samuel 1:26), and Gideon before the Angel of the Lord (Judges 6:13).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when we came to the inn, that we opened our sacks, and, behold, every man's money was in the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight: and we have brought it again in our hand.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers explain what happened on the way home. “When we came to the inn, … we opened our sacks, and, behold, every man’s money was in the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight.” The narrative of chapter 42 told how one brother found his money at the lodging place and the rest found theirs at home (42:27, 35). Here the brothers compress the story and speak as though all the money was found at the inn. They are summarizing, not lying; their point is that every man’s silver came back, and they want to settle the account completely.

The word “inn” refers to a stopping place on the road, not a building with rooms and an innkeeper but a campsite or shelter where travellers rested and fed their animals. It was there, as one brother opened his sack for fodder, that the first discovery was made.

“Our money in full weight” describes silver measured exactly. Money in the patriarchal age was not coined but weighed out in pieces of silver, as when Abraham weighed four hundred shekels for the cave of Machpelah (23:16). The brothers insist that nothing had been deducted. Then comes the vital statement: “we have brought it again in our hand.” They are making full restitution, openly and voluntarily. Men once willing to sell a brother for twenty pieces of silver (37:28) now insist on returning silver that came to them without their asking. Honesty in small things shows a heart turning in a new direction (Luke 16:10).

wordNotes.term: הַמָּלוֹן (hammalon) — the inn
wordNotes.explanation: Malon, from lun, “to lodge, spend the night,” is a place for overnight stopping on a journey, likely an open campsite or simple shelter. It is where the first sack was opened (42:27) and where the Lord met Moses on his journey back to Egypt (Exodus 4:24). Jeremiah longs for a “lodging place of wayfaring men” in the wilderness (Jeremiah 9:2).

wordNotes.term: בְּמִשְׁקָלוֹ (bemishqalo) — in full weight
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “according to its weight.” Silver was weighed on scales rather than counted as coins, and the law later required just weights and balances (Leviticus 19:36). The phrase assures the steward that the whole amount is present, as at Ezra’s careful weighing of temple treasure (Ezra 8:34).

verses.bibleText: And other money have we brought down in our hands to buy food: we cannot tell who put our money in our sacks.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And other money have we brought down in our hands to buy food.” The brothers make clear that the returned silver is not their payment for new grain. They have brought separate money for the current purchase. They are not trying to use Egypt’s own silver to buy Egypt’s grain.

Then comes a candid admission: “we cannot tell who put our money in our sacks.” They offer no theory and blame no one. When the money first appeared, they trembled and asked what God was doing to them (42:28). Now they confess simple ignorance. They have no explanation and do not pretend to have one.

That confession of not knowing prepares for the steward’s reply in the next verse. The brothers can only say who did not put the money there; the steward will tell them who did, in terms they could never have guessed. Human understanding reaches its limit, and an answer from God’s side fills the gap. The pattern runs through the Joseph story: events whose cause is hidden turn out to be the work of a hand the participants cannot see (45:8; 50:20).

wordNotes.term: לֹא יָדַעְנוּ מִי־שָׂם (lo’ yada‘nu mi-sam) — we cannot tell who put
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “we do not know who placed.” The verb sim, “to put, to set,” is used again when Joseph orders the money placed in the sacks a second time (44:1-2) and when the food is “set on” at the meal (v. 31). The brothers’ honest ignorance contrasts with the steward’s confident explanation (v. 23). Proverbs asks, “how can a man then understand his own way?” (Proverbs 20:24).

verses.bibleText: And he said, Peace be to you, fear not: your God, and the God of your father, hath given you treasure in your sacks: I had your money. And he brought Simeon out unto them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The steward’s answer turns the chapter. “Peace be to you, fear not.” The brothers braced for accusation and receive a greeting of peace. The word shalom carries far more than calm: it means welfare, wholeness, and right relationship. The brothers who once “could not speak peaceably” to Joseph (37:4) now hear peace pronounced over them in Joseph’s own house. The words “fear not” are the kind spoken to people trembling before a power they cannot resist, and in Scripture they often come from God or his messengers (15:1; Judges 6:23).

Then comes an explanation that must have bewildered them: “your God, and the God of your father, hath given you treasure in your sacks.” An Egyptian official speaks of the brothers’ God and their father’s God, using covenant-family language. He had evidently learned it from Joseph, who openly confessed the God of his fathers in Egypt (41:16, 25, 51-52). The steward knows the source of the money, since he likely put it there himself at Joseph’s command (42:25). Yet his explanation is not a mere cover story. Behind the human act of returning the money stood the gracious purpose of the God who was preserving this family. The steward may have spoken more truth than he understood.

The word he uses is not “money” but “treasure,” a word for something hidden and valuable, found unexpectedly. The brothers’ silver came back to them as a gift, and the gift was meant to show kindness, not to trap them. The brothers had asked, “What is this that God hath done unto us?” (42:28), fearing judgment. The answer is that God had done them good.

“I had your money” is the formal receipt of an accountant: the payment came to me, the books are balanced, there is no debt. The brothers’ fear of being charged with theft is removed in a single phrase. Then, as proof that no case is pending against them, “he brought Simeon out unto them.” The hostage is released, and the eleven brothers stand together again for the first time in many months.

The scene foreshadows the way grace works. People burdened with guilt expect accusation; God meets them with peace, declares the account settled, and restores what was lost. The risen Christ’s first word to his frightened disciples was “Peace be unto you” (John 20:19). Paul writes that being justified by faith we have peace with God (Romans 5:1), a peace grounded not in the sinner’s innocence but in a payment already received.

wordNotes.term: שָׁלוֹם לָכֶם אַל־תִּירָאוּ (shalom lakhem ’al-tira’u) — peace be to you, fear not
wordNotes.explanation: Shalom denotes wholeness and well-being, and in a greeting it declares that no hostility exists between speaker and hearer. Paired with “fear not,” it calms people who expect harm. The Lord speaks the same words to Gideon (Judges 6:23), and the risen Jesus greets his disciples with “Peace be unto you” (Luke 24:36). In this chapter shalom recurs in Joseph’s inquiry after his brothers’ welfare (vv. 27-28), tracing the restoration of a broken family.

wordNotes.term: מַטְמוֹן (matmon) — treasure
wordNotes.explanation: Matmon refers to hidden treasure, wealth stored or buried away. Job speaks of those who long for death more than for “hid treasures” (Job 3:21); Proverbs urges seeking wisdom as for hidden treasures (Proverbs 2:4); God promises Cyrus “hidden riches of secret places” (Isaiah 45:3). The steward’s choice of word turns returned silver into a gift with a hidden giver, hinting at God’s concealed working throughout the story.

verses.bibleText: And the man brought the men into Joseph's house, and gave them water, and they washed their feet; and he gave their asses provender.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The steward now treats the brothers as honoured guests. “The man brought the men into Joseph’s house, and gave them water, and they washed their feet; and he gave their asses provender.” Each act answers one of their fears. They worried they would be taken as slaves; instead they are given water to wash like free guests. They worried they would lose their donkeys; instead the animals are fed.

Foot-washing was the first courtesy of hospitality in a land of dusty roads and open sandals. Abraham offered water to his three visitors at Mamre (18:4), Lot to the two angels at Sodom (19:2), and Laban’s household to Abraham’s servant and his men (24:32). Providing fodder for animals was part of the same courtesy (24:25, 32). By offering both, the steward signals that the brothers are welcomed, not detained.

The New Testament gives foot-washing a deeper meaning. Jesus washed his disciples’ feet as a sign of humble, cleansing love and told them to do the same for one another (John 13:5, 14-15). Hospitality to strangers is still a mark of godliness (1 Timothy 5:10; Hebrews 13:2). In Joseph’s house, men who sold their brother receive kindness they did not earn, and they receive it before they understand who is giving it.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּרְחֲצוּ רַגְלֵיהֶם (vayyirchatsu raglehem) — and they washed their feet
wordNotes.explanation: Rachats, “to wash,” is used for the customary washing of travellers’ feet on arrival, a basic act of welcome (18:4; 19:2; 24:32). Abigail offers to wash the feet of David’s servants as a sign of humble service (1 Samuel 25:41). Jesus takes up the practice at the Last Supper, washing the disciples’ feet himself (John 13:5).

verses.bibleText: And they made ready the present against Joseph came at noon: for they heard that they should eat bread there.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they made ready the present against Joseph came at noon.” With their fears eased, the brothers turn to the task of preparing their gift. They arrange the balm, honey, spices, myrrh, nuts, and almonds so that they can present them properly when the governor arrives. The word for “made ready” suggests careful setting out, as one would display tribute before a dignitary.

The reason for their preparation is given: “for they heard that they should eat bread there.” For the first time they learn the true purpose of their visit to the house. They are not prisoners but dinner guests. To “eat bread” meant to share a meal, and sharing a meal in the ancient Near East established fellowship and goodwill between host and guest.

The scene echoes the past. After throwing Joseph into the pit, the brothers “sat down to eat bread” while he cried out below (37:25). Now they will eat bread at Joseph’s own table. The meal they ate in callousness is answered by a meal given in grace.

wordNotes.term: יֹאכְלוּ לָחֶם (yo’khelu lachem) — they should eat bread
wordNotes.explanation: To “eat bread” is an idiom for sharing a meal, often sealing friendship or covenant. Jacob and Laban “did eat bread” on the mount after making their covenant (31:54). The brothers once sat down “to eat bread” beside the pit (37:25). In the Gospels a guest at a meal exclaims, “Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke 14:15).

verses.bibleText: And when Joseph came home, they brought him the present which was in their hand into the house, and bowed themselves to him to the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when Joseph came home, they brought him the present which was in their hand into the house, and bowed themselves to him to the earth.” This is the moment the dreams of chapter 37 reach their fulfilment in full. In the first journey ten brothers bowed before Joseph (42:6). Now Benjamin is among them, and with Simeon restored, all eleven brothers prostrate themselves before the one they had mocked as “this dreamer” (37:19).

Joseph’s first dream showed eleven sheaves bowing to his sheaf (37:7). The brothers had reacted with fury: “Shalt thou indeed reign over us?” (37:8). They sold him precisely to prevent such a thing, and they have unwittingly brought it about. Their own actions became the means of fulfilling what they tried to defeat. God’s word does not fail, even when people strive to make it fail. Psalm 105 says that “the word of the LORD tried him” until the time came for it to be fulfilled (Psalm 105:19).

The brothers also bring their gift, the minchah Jacob prepared. Balm, spices, and myrrh, the goods that once rode down to Egypt on the camels of the traders who bought Joseph, are now laid before Joseph by the hands that sold him. Presenting tribute while bowing to the ground is the posture of subjects before a ruler. The brothers do not know they are bowing to their brother; they know only that their lives and their family’s survival rest in this man’s hands.

The scene points ahead to a greater fulfilment. The brothers who rejected Joseph eventually bowed to him and found that he was their saviour. Scripture foresees a day when every knee will bow to the One once rejected by his own (Philippians 2:10-11), and blessed are those who bow in trust before they are compelled to bow in judgment.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ־לוֹ אָרְצָה (vayyishtachavu-lo ’artsah) — and bowed themselves to him to the earth
wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes full prostration, bowing face to the ground before a superior or before God. It is the word used in Joseph’s dreams for the sheaves and stars bowing to him (37:7, 9), and when the brothers bowed on their first visit (42:6). The same verb will describe their bowing in verse 28 and again in 50:18, where they offer themselves as his servants.

verses.bibleText: And he asked them of their welfare, and said, Is your father well, the old man of whom ye spake? Is he yet alive?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph begins with courtesy. “He asked them of their welfare, and said, Is your father well, the old man of whom ye spake? Is he yet alive?” The word translated “welfare” and “well” is shalom, the same word the steward used in his greeting. Joseph asks about the brothers’ shalom and then about his father’s shalom.

The question about their welfare reverses an old wound. Years before, Jacob had sent Joseph to Shechem to “see whether it be well [shalom] with thy brethren” (37:14). He found them, and they answered his errand of peace with a plot to kill him. Now the roles are reversed, and Joseph again asks after their shalom, this time with the power to destroy them and the will to bless them.

The question about Jacob is carefully framed: “the old man of whom ye spake.” Joseph disguises his longing by referring to what they told him earlier, so that his interest seems natural for a ruler recalling a conversation. Yet his second question betrays his heart: “Is he yet alive?” That is the question of a son who has wondered for twenty-two years whether his father still lives. When Joseph finally reveals himself, it will be the first thing he asks: “Doth my father yet live?” (45:3).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁאַל לָהֶם לְשָׁלוֹם (vayyish’al lahem leshalom) — and he asked them of their welfare
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “he asked them about peace.” The idiom refers to inquiring after someone’s health and circumstances, as Jacob asks about Laban (29:6) and Moses about Jethro (Exodus 18:7). In the Joseph story the word shalom carries special weight: the brothers could not speak to Joseph “peaceably” (37:4), and Jacob sent him to see their shalom (37:14). Joseph now offers what was once refused him.

verses.bibleText: And they answered, Thy servant our father is in good health, he is yet alive. And they bowed down their heads, and made obeisance.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they answered, Thy servant our father is in good health, he is yet alive.” The brothers repeat the word shalom: their father is “in peace,” well and living. Without knowing it, they give Joseph the news he has longed to hear.

They call Jacob “thy servant our father.” The phrase is ordinary court courtesy, but in this setting it carries irony. Joseph’s second dream showed the sun and moon as well as eleven stars bowing to him (37:9), and Jacob had rebuked him: “Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee?” (37:10). Now his sons call their father the servant of the very son he rebuked.

Then “they bowed down their heads, and made obeisance.” This is the second time in the chapter that they bow, and the double verbs suggest a deep, deliberate reverence. Some take it as thanks to Joseph for his concern; it may also be a gesture of gratitude to God that their father still lived. Whatever its intent, the brothers again fulfil the dreams they once despised, bowing low before the brother they believe they will never see again.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקְּדוּ וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲוּוּ (vayyiqqedu vayyishtachavu) — and they bowed down their heads, and made obeisance
wordNotes.explanation: Qadad means to bow the head, and shachah (in this form) to prostrate oneself. The pair often appears in worship or deep reverence: Abraham’s servant bowed his head and worshipped when God led him to Rebekah (24:26), and Israel did the same when they heard the Lord had visited them (Exodus 4:31; 12:27). Here the gesture is directed toward Joseph, but the language hints at gratitude reaching beyond him.

verses.bibleText: And he lifted up his eyes, and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother's son, and said, Is this your younger brother, of whom ye spake unto me? And he said, God be gracious unto thee, my son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he lifted up his eyes, and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother’s son.” The narrator slows the moment to a single look. Joseph has already noticed Benjamin (v. 16), but now, at close range and in his own house, he looks fully at the brother he last saw as a boy. The phrase “lifted up his eyes” often introduces a significant sight in Genesis (22:4, 13; 24:63-64), and “his mother’s son” stresses the bond between them. Of all the brothers, only Benjamin shares Rachel as mother.

Joseph asks a question he already knows the answer to: “Is this your younger brother, of whom ye spake unto me?” Once again he refers to their earlier words, keeping his interest disguised. Then, before they can answer, he pronounces a blessing: “God be gracious unto thee, my son.”

The words are remarkable. The phrase “God be gracious” will later form part of the priestly blessing Aaron pronounces over Israel (Numbers 6:25). It is not a common greeting; it is a blessing invoked from the heart. Calling Benjamin “my son” would sound natural from an older official to a younger man, but it carries far more for Joseph, who is speaking to his own brother.

The verb for grace links back to the brothers’ confession in the previous chapter. They remembered that Joseph “besought” them in the anguish of his soul and they would not hear (42:21). That word is from the same root: Joseph pleaded for grace and was refused. Now he pronounces God’s grace over Benjamin. Instead of returning harm for harm, he gives the blessing that he was once denied. This is the spirit Jesus taught when he told his followers to bless those who curse them (Luke 6:28), and the spirit he showed when he prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34).

wordNotes.term: אֱלֹהִים יָחְנְךָ בְּנִי (’Elohim yochnekha beni) — God be gracious unto thee, my son
wordNotes.explanation: Chanan means to show favour or grace, especially undeserved kindness from a superior. The prayer anticipates the priestly blessing, “The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee” (Numbers 6:25), and the psalmist’s “God be merciful unto us” (Psalm 67:1). The reflexive form of the same verb described Joseph pleading with his brothers for mercy in the pit (42:21). Beni, “my son,” is an affectionate address to a younger person (1 Samuel 3:16).

wordNotes.term: בֶּן־אִמּוֹ (ben-’immo) — his mother’s son
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase identifies a full brother, sharing both parents. In a household with several wives it marked a closer bond than shared fatherhood alone. Gideon’s grief for “my brethren, even the sons of my mother” shows the depth of that tie (Judges 8:19), and the law speaks of “thy brother, the son of thy mother” as one of the closest relations (Deuteronomy 13:6). Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin (35:18), so he and Joseph were all that remained of her.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph made haste; for his bowels did yearn upon his brother: and he sought where to weep; and he entered into his chamber, and wept there.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph made haste; for his bowels did yearn upon his brother.” The composure Joseph has kept through two audiences finally breaks. The blessing he has just spoken over Benjamin opens a floodgate of feeling, and he must leave the room before it overwhelms him in front of everyone. The haste is the hurry of a man who knows that in another moment he will weep openly and give himself away.

The KJV’s “bowels did yearn” reflects the Hebrew idiom literally: his inner parts “grew warm” or were “stirred.” The ancient Hebrews located the deepest emotions in the inward organs, much as English speaks of the heart. The noun is rachamim, the same word Jacob used in his prayer that God Almighty would give his sons “mercy” before the man (v. 14). Jacob prayed for compassion, and the compassion of the man in Egypt now overflows, though not in the way Jacob imagined. The same expression describes the true mother before Solomon, whose “bowels yearned upon her son” when the king threatened to divide the child (1 Kings 3:26). Hosea uses related language for God himself: “my repentings are kindled together” as he refuses to give up Ephraim (Hosea 11:8). Joseph’s love for Benjamin has the protective tenderness of a parent’s love, perhaps all the stronger because their mother died bringing Benjamin into the world.

“And he sought where to weep; and he entered into his chamber, and wept there.” This is the second of Joseph’s recorded weepings. He wept when he heard his brothers confess their guilt (42:24); he will weep aloud when he reveals himself (45:2) and again as he embraces Benjamin and the others (45:14-15), and once more after Jacob’s death when his brothers fear his revenge (50:17). Each time his tears show that the stern exterior is a mask worn for a purpose. He is testing his brothers, not punishing them, and the test costs him dearly.

The hidden tears of Joseph give a glimpse of something true about God. When the Lord seems distant or severe, his heart is not cold. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35) and over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). In the parable, the father saw his returning son from afar and “had compassion” and ran to him (Luke 15:20). Christ, our high priest, is “touched with the feeling of our infirmities” (Hebrews 4:15). Behind providences that feel hard there is a love that weeps in secret and waits for the right moment to make itself known.

wordNotes.term: כִּי־נִכְמְרוּ רַחֲמָיו (ki-nikhmeru rachamav) — for his bowels did yearn
wordNotes.explanation: Nikhmeru comes from a verb meaning to grow warm or be stirred, and rachamav is “his compassions,” from the word linked to rechem, “womb.” The phrase describes intense tender emotion welling up inside. It is used of the mother pleading for her child before Solomon (1 Kings 3:26) and, with a related form, of God’s own compassion for wayward Ephraim (Hosea 11:8). The Greek of the Gospels uses a corresponding word for Jesus’ compassion on the crowds (Matthew 9:36).

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּבְךְּ שָׁמָּה (vayyevk shammah) — and wept there
wordNotes.explanation: Bakah, “to weep,” recurs at every stage of Joseph’s reconciliation with his family (42:24; 45:2, 14-15; 46:29; 50:17). Here the weeping is private, in his chamber, hidden from the brothers. The word reveals the cost of Joseph’s restraint and the depth of his love.

verses.bibleText: And he washed his face, and went out, and refrained himself, and said, Set on bread.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he washed his face, and went out, and refrained himself.” Joseph removes the traces of his tears and returns to the hall. The verb “refrained himself” describes a deliberate act of holding back powerful emotion by force of will. Joseph has not stopped feeling; he has chosen not to show it yet. When he finally can no longer restrain himself, the same verb will mark the moment of revelation: “Then Joseph could not refrain himself” (45:1).

The reason for the restraint is the test still underway. Joseph has seen that his brothers brought Benjamin, returned the money, and spoken honestly. He has not yet seen how they will act when Benjamin is favoured over them or when Benjamin’s life is at stake. To reveal himself now would cut the process short and leave unanswered the question of whether they have truly changed. Love sometimes waits for the sake of the beloved.

“And said, Set on bread.” The command is brief and businesslike, the voice of the governor once again. The meal that will form the next stage of the test begins. There is a lesson in Joseph’s self-mastery for anyone who must act wisely amid strong feelings. Proverbs commends the one who “ruleth his spirit” above the one who takes a city (Proverbs 16:32).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּתְאַפַּק (vayyit’appaq) — and refrained himself
wordNotes.explanation: The reflexive form of ’aphaq means to restrain oneself, to hold in one’s feelings. Joseph “could not refrain himself” when he finally made himself known (45:1). Haman “refrained himself” from venting his rage at Mordecai (Esther 5:10), and the Lord speaks of having long “refrained myself” before acting for his people (Isaiah 42:14).

verses.bibleText: And they set on for him by himself, and for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians, which did eat with him, by themselves: because the Egyptians might not eat bread with the Hebrews; for that is an abomination unto the Egyptians.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they set on for him by himself, and for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians, which did eat with him, by themselves.” The meal is served at three separate places. Joseph eats alone, as his rank requires; the brothers eat together; and the Egyptians of Joseph’s household eat by themselves. The arrangement reflects both Joseph’s exalted position and the strict social divisions of Egypt.

The narrator explains the separation: “because the Egyptians might not eat bread with the Hebrews; for that is an abomination unto the Egyptians.” Egyptians regarded themselves as the true people and other nations as lesser. Ancient writers report that Egyptians would not use a foreigner’s knife or cooking pot, nor eat meat cut by a foreign hand, and that they held certain animals sacred which other peoples ate. Later in the story Joseph tells his brothers that “every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians” (46:34), and Moses warns Pharaoh that Israel’s sacrifices would be an abomination in Egyptian eyes (Exodus 8:26).

This prejudice is human custom, not God’s law. It should not be confused with the distinction between clean and unclean foods that God gave his people, which rests on his word and concerns what is fit to eat, not which nations may share a table. Israel was to keep that distinction while being reminded to love the stranger (Deuteronomy 10:19).

In God’s providence, this very contempt served a purpose. In Canaan the family had been drifting into intermarriage and assimilation, as Judah’s story in chapter 38 showed. In Egypt they would be kept apart, settled in Goshen and unlikely to merge with their hosts. The separation that seemed like a slight became a shelter in which a family could grow into a nation.

The gospel answers such walls between peoples. Peter learned that God had shown him “that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Acts 10:28), and Paul declares that Christ has broken down “the middle wall of partition” (Ephesians 2:14). At the table of the Lord, Hebrew and Egyptian, Jew and Gentile sit together (Galatians 3:28).

wordNotes.term: תּוֹעֵבָה (to‘evah) — an abomination
wordNotes.explanation: To‘evah denotes something regarded as detestable or offensive. In this verse and in 46:34 and Exodus 8:26 the standard is Egyptian custom: the Egyptians found it abhorrent to share food with Hebrews or to live near shepherds. Elsewhere in Scripture the same word describes what God himself declares abominable, including unclean foods (Deuteronomy 14:3) and idolatry. Context shows whose judgment is in view.

wordNotes.term: הָעִבְרִים (ha‘ivrim) — the Hebrews
wordNotes.explanation: “Hebrew” is the term outsiders often used for Abraham’s descendants. Abram is the first so called (14:13). Potiphar’s wife used it contemptuously of Joseph (39:14, 17), and the chief butler called him “a young man, an Hebrew” (41:12). The word marked the family as foreigners in Egypt.

verses.bibleText: And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth: and the men marvelled one at another.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth.” The brothers find themselves seated in exact order of age, from Reuben down to Benjamin. They had not been asked their ages. Several were born to different mothers within a few years of one another, and even a well-informed observer would have had difficulty arranging them correctly. Yet the seating is precise.

“And the men marvelled one at another.” They look at each other in astonishment. How could an Egyptian ruler know such details? The arrangement must have seemed uncanny, as though the man could see into their family history. It adds to the unsettling sense that nothing about them is hidden from him. Joseph is deliberately allowing them to feel that their secrets lie open before a knowing eye, a feeling that will grow when he speaks of divination in the next chapter (44:15).

The seating also has a pointed significance. Rank by birth had been a source of conflict throughout the family’s history. Esau sold his birthright to Jacob (25:31-34), Jacob received the blessing intended for the elder (27:36), and Joseph, the eleventh son, had been raised above his older brothers by Jacob’s favour. The brothers are now seated with the youngest at the bottom, in the order of nature. Then, in the next verse, the youngest will be honoured most. Joseph sets the stage so that favouritism toward Benjamin will stand out clearly against the backdrop of ordered rank.

The astonishment of the brothers at being known is a small echo of what every person will experience before God. “All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do” (Hebrews 4:13). For the guilty that knowledge is fearful; for those who have been forgiven it becomes the comfort of being fully known and still loved.

wordNotes.term: הַבְּכֹר כִּבְכֹרָתוֹ וְהַצָּעִיר כִּצְעִרָתוֹ (habbekhor kivkhorato vehatsa‘ir kits‘irato) — the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth
wordNotes.explanation: Bekhorah, “birthright,” is the right of the firstborn that Esau despised (25:31-34). Tsa‘ir, “young, small,” refers to the youngest. The phrasing balances the two ends of the line. Genesis repeatedly shows God overturning birth order, choosing Jacob over Esau and later Ephraim over Manasseh (48:14), and Reuben will lose the firstborn’s privileges (49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּתְמְהוּ (vayyitmehu) — and they marvelled
wordNotes.explanation: Tamah means to be astonished or amazed, often with a sense of bewilderment or alarm. Kings who saw Zion “marvelled” and were troubled (Psalm 48:5), and Habakkuk is told to “wonder marvellously” at what God is doing (Habakkuk 1:5). The brothers’ amazement suggests unease more than delight.

verses.bibleText: And he took and sent messes unto them from before him: but Benjamin's mess was five times so much as any of their's. And they drank, and were merry with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he took and sent messes unto them from before him.” A “mess” is an old English word for a portion of food. Joseph, eating at his own table, sends servings from his table to his brothers.
