Sending portions from the host’s table was a mark of honour; Samuel set aside a special portion for Saul at the feast where he was to be anointed (1 Samuel 9:23-24), and David sent a portion from the king’s table after Uriah (2 Samuel 11:8).

“But Benjamin’s mess was five times so much as any of their’s.” Here lies the test. Joseph openly favours the youngest son of Rachel, as Jacob once openly favoured Joseph with the coat of many colours (37:3). That favouritism had stirred the brothers to hatred and violence (37:4, 18-28). Would the same envy rise again? The number five need not carry any hidden meaning; it simply marks a lavish, unmistakable distinction. Joseph will later show the same generosity, giving Benjamin five changes of clothing and three hundred pieces of silver (45:22).

The brothers pass this test. “And they drank, and were merry with him.” No grumbling is recorded, no resentful glances, no plotting. They share the meal in good spirits, even though Benjamin receives the greater honour. The men who could not bear to see Joseph preferred can now rejoice when Benjamin is preferred.

The phrase “were merry” must be handled with care. The Hebrew verb often means to become drunk, as with Noah (9:21), but it can also describe drinking one’s fill, enjoying satisfaction and plenty. Haggai uses it of people who drink but are “not filled with drink” (Haggai 1:6), and the Song of Solomon calls lovers to “drink abundantly” (Song of Solomon 5:1). In this context of a feast after famine, the emphasis falls on contentment and celebration, not intoxication. The narrator describes what happened without commending it, and the rest of Scripture is clear that strong drink deceives and that God’s people are to be sober and temperate (Proverbs 20:1; 23:29-32; Ephesians 5:18).

The scene ends in apparent peace, but Joseph has one more test prepared. The brothers have shown that they will not resent Benjamin’s honour; they must still show whether they will abandon him in danger. That trial awaits in the next chapter.

wordNotes.term: מַשְׂאֹת (mas’ot) — messes, portions
wordNotes.explanation: Mas’et, from nasa’, “to lift, carry,” refers to a portion lifted and carried to someone, often a gift of honour from a superior’s table. David sent a mas’et after Uriah (2 Samuel 11:8), and Esther’s king gave gifts “according to the state of the king” (Esther 2:18). Benjamin’s fivefold portion marked him as the guest of highest honour.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁכְּרוּ (vayyishkeru) — and were merry
wordNotes.explanation: Shakhar often means to become drunk (9:21), but it can describe drinking freely to satisfaction, as in Haggai 1:6, where people drink but are not “filled with drink,” and Song of Solomon 5:1, “drink abundantly.” In this festal setting the sense is relaxed contentment and plenty. Scripture elsewhere warns firmly against intoxication (Proverbs 23:29-32).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does it take to trust God with the person or thing you are most afraid of losing?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Under the pressure of famine God brings Jacob to surrender, raises Judah to stake his own life for his brother, and meets frightened, guilty men with peace and a meal before they understand who their host is.
discussionQuestions: How does Judah’s offer in verses 8-9 differ from Reuben’s in 42:37, and what does the difference reveal about Judah?
Jacob prays for God’s mercy and in the same breath resigns himself to loss; is verse 14 faith, fatalism, or both?
Why do the brothers immediately suspect a trap when they are invited to dine, and what does their fear say about a guilty conscience?
What did the steward mean by saying their God had given them treasure, and how does that speak of grace received before it is understood?
Why does Joseph weep in private and then return to test his brothers further?
commonMisunderstandings: Judah’s pledge does not contradict Proverbs’ warnings against rash suretyship; he binds himself for his own brother to save the whole family.
Jacob’s “if I be bereaved, I am bereaved” is not stoic indifference; it follows a prayer to God Almighty and marks the surrender of what he could no longer control.
The note that the brothers “were merry” does not commend drunkenness; the phrase describes festive plenty, and Scripture elsewhere warns plainly against strong drink.
The Egyptian refusal to eat with Hebrews is a social and religious prejudice, not the clean and unclean distinction God gave his people.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep Judah’s pledge at the centre: a brother who once sold Joseph now offers himself for Benjamin, a pattern brought to perfection in Christ, the surety of a better covenant.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: The God who turned Jacob’s fear into a feast asks us to place in his hands what we hold most tightly, and to rest on the One who became surety for us.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Christ our surety: as Judah bound his own life to bring Benjamin safely to his father, Jesus pledged himself for sinners and brings them home to the Father.
flow: Famine left Jacob’s family with no way to live unless Benjamin went down to Egypt.
Judah stepped forward and said, “I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him.”
Jacob let go of his son and committed the outcome to God Almighty.
In Egypt the guilty brothers were met with peace, released brothers, and a feast they did not earn.
Jesus, of Judah’s tribe, is the surety who answers for us and the host who welcomes us to his table.
simpleIllustrations: A co-signer on a loan puts his own name and property behind another person’s debt; Judah co-signed with his life.
A child who clenches a broken toy cannot receive the new one in a parent’s hand until the fist opens.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you rest your case on Jesus, who has pledged himself for you, and place in God’s hands what you are most afraid to lose?
cautions: Do not allegorize every detail of the meal; keep the Christ connection to the clear pattern of a brother who stakes himself for another.
Do not use verse 34 to excuse drinking; present the biblical counsel on temperance plainly where the subject arises.

reflectionQuestions: What am I holding so tightly that I have not yet entrusted it to God Almighty?
Am I willing, like Judah, to take responsibility for someone else’s good at cost to myself?
When God’s kindness surprises me, do I meet it with suspicion because of my own guilt?
Where might God be giving me “treasure in my sack” that I have not yet recognized as his gift?
Can I rejoice when someone else is favoured more than I am?
